extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and public administration; legislators and administrators interested in U.S. local government
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the principles, institutions, and practical effects of local administration in the United States (township, county, courts, elections, and executive functions). Aims to identify mechanisms of enforcement, variation between States, and political consequences of administrative arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of enforcing execution of the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, society has only two methods of enforcing the execution of the laws at its disposal: a discretionary power may be entrusted to a superior functionary of directing all the others, and of cashiering them in case of disobedience; or the courts of justice may be authorized to inflict judicial penalties on the offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both methods are not always available; the text repeatedly compares their availability and consequences in different institutional settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inalienability of elective functions
rubrics_metrics.description: An elected magistrate can neither be cashiered nor promoted. All elective functions are inalienable until their term is expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because elected officials cannot be removed or rewarded by a superior, the double right of commanding and enforcing obedience cannot be vested in the same individual, producing administrative dispersion and requiring other checks (notably judicial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional extension of judicial power to elective offices
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be in the exact ratio of the extension of elective offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If judicial oversight does not grow with elective offices, an elective authority not subject to judicial power will either elude control or be destroyed; courts are the only medium to compel elected functionaries to obey without violating electors' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts of justice as the medium between central power and administrative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts of justice are the only possible medium between the central power and the administrative bodies; they alone can compel the elected functionary to obey, without violating the rights of the elector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames judicial remedies (fines, mandates, appointments) as instruments that substitute for hierarchical administrative control where elections prevent removal or promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of Justices of the Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The Justice of the Peace is a sort of mezzo termine between the magistrate and the man of the world... His office simply obliges him to execute the police regulations of society; a task in which good sense and integrity are of more avail than legal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justices introduce formalities and publicity into administration, resist despotism, and perform both administrative and semi-judicial tasks; U.S. adoption removes aristocratic character and adapts functions to local needs (appointing Courts of Sessions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Sessions' dual administrative and judicial function
rubrics_metrics.description: In Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at the same time an administrative body, properly so called, and a political tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It meets twice a year, enforces obedience of many public officers, presides over county affairs that concern multiple townships, and in township matters acts judicially; its mixed role provides administrative oversight while borrowing judicial forms for information and guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of judicial penalties to ensure township compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a township attempts to evade the payment of the taxes by neglecting to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions condemns it to a heavy penalty. The fine is levied on each of the inhabitants; and the sheriff of the county ... executes the mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial sentences conceal governmental authority and leverage the coercive power of law to compel local compliance with statewide obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of public-officer misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: All the reprehensible actions of which a public functionary may be guilty are reducible to the following heads: He may execute the law without energy or zeal; He may neglect to execute the law; He may do what the law enjoins him not to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the last two (neglect and positive unlawful acts) give rise to judicial cognizance; mere lack of zeal or ability is not typically subject to legal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a positive and appreciable fact for judicial action
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive and appreciable fact is the indispensable foundation of an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cannot compel better performance where duties are performed inadequately but lawfully; enforcement typically requires tangible legal violations or formal procedures (fines, prosecutions, appointments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal as the primary check on quasi-offences
rubrics_metrics.description: The only security of that active and enlightened obedience which a court of justice cannot impose upon public officers lies in the possibility of their arbitrary removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts cannot enforce zeal or competence, administrative systems rely on removal powers (executive in some countries, electoral mechanisms in the U.S.) to deter quasi-offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of inspection and prosecution to limit concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have therefore divided the offices of inspection and of prosecution, as well as all the other functions of the administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than appointing a single powerful public prosecutor with township agents (which would concentrate power), the U.S. disperses duties: grand jurors inform, fiscal officers may prosecute, and private plaintiffs are often empowered to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on private interest and informers to secure enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: American legislation... appeals to the private interest of the citizen... Reduced by their system to this extremity, the Americans are obliged to encourage informers by bestowing on them a portion of the penalty in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws commonly allow private individuals to bring prosecutions and award them portions of fines (e.g., half the fine) to incentivize enforcement where collective action problems or low individual stakes would otherwise prevent suits; the author notes moral dangers of this expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal characteristics of the American administrative system
rubrics_metrics.description: The election of public officers, or the inalienability of their functions, the absence of a gradation of powers, and the introduction of a judicial control over the secondary branches of the administration, are the universal characteristics of the American system from Maine to the Floridas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features combine across the Union even as statutory details vary by State; they explain why judicial remedies and penalties are widely used to regulate local functionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic variation in local administrative activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more we descend towards the South, the less active does the business of the township or parish become; the number of magistrates, of functions, and of rights decreases; the population exercises a less immediate influence on affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In northern and northwestern States (New England, Ohio) townships remain active; in New York, Pennsylvania, and southern States the county gains prominence and local participation wanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: County assemblies as instruments of centralizing local administration
rubrics_metrics.description: In the State of New York, on the contrary, and in those of Ohio and Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county choose a certain number of representatives, who constitute the assembly of the county. The county assembly has the right of taxing the inhabitants to a certain extent; ... it exercises an executive power in the county, frequently directs the administration of the townships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with Massachusetts model where county business is conducted by appointed Court of Sessions and budget is voted by the State; county assemblies introduce a representative, partially legislative-executive county layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a dependent series of public functionaries (no gradation of ranks)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the officers are everywhere elected or appointed for a certain period, it has been impossible to establish the rules of a dependent series of authorities; there are almost as many independent functionaries as there are functions, and the executive power is disseminated in a multitude of hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dispersion necessitates judicial control and pecuniary penalties to enforce compliance and compensates for lack of hierarchical oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between central government and administrative centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization of government (directing general interests) is different from centralization of the local administration (directing partial or local interests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two forms can co-exist but are separable; the author argues a strong central government is necessary for national action while centralized administration may erode public spirit and local initiative—examples: Louis XIV (central government strong, administration less centralized) and England (central government strong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and benefits of dividing the legislature into two Houses
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of the legislative power and the consequent check upon political assemblies; with the creation of a tribunal of appeal for the revision of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate generally fewer members, longer terms, may have executive and judicial roles (nominations, trial of political offences); House of Representatives has shorter terms and limited roles (impeachment). The bicameral division preserves experienced nucleus of lawmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's constitutional role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Governor is the official moderator and counsellor of the legislature. He is armed with a veto or suspensive power... He is the commander of the militia, and head of the armed force... The Governor takes no share in the administration of townships and counties, except it be indirectly in the nomination of Justices of the Peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically the Governor may name agents to execute measures; his short term and elective status make him dependent on the people; in some States he does not appoint justices of the peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political effects of extensive local administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Local authority has been carried to lengths which no European nation could endure without great inconvenience... But in the United States the centralization of the Government is complete... The great authorities of the State have the right of watching and controlling the subordinate agents, without that of rewarding or punishing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination yields a powerful central government amid highly independent local administrations, producing both advantages (national cohesion, local attentiveness to interests) and disadvantages (reduced public spirit in localities, enforcement difficulties).
